solution:
The internuclear axis is taken as the \(x\)-axis. A sigma \((\sigma)\) bond requires end-to-end, or head-on, overlap of the two orbitals along that axis. If instead the two orbital axes are parallel to each other and perpendicular to the internuclear axis, the lobes can only meet sidewise, and the overlap gives a pi \((\pi)\) bond.

The combination that fails is the one between two \(2p_y\) orbitals. A \(2p_y\) orbital has its lobes directed along the \(y\)-axis, so on each of the two atoms the orbital axis is perpendicular to the internuclear \(x\)-axis. The two axes are therefore parallel to one another and at right angles to the line joining the nuclei, which is exactly the condition for lateral overlap: the lobes approach each other sideways and produce two saucer-shaped charge clouds lying above and below the plane of the atoms. That is a \(\pi\) bond, not a \(\sigma\) bond. Note the two \(2p_y\) orbitals do still bond, and the resulting \(\pi\) bond is weaker than a \(\sigma\) bond because sidewise overlap is less extensive than axial overlap.

Each of the other three combinations overlaps head-on along the internuclear axis and so does give a \(\sigma\) bond.

For \(1s\) with \(1s\): an \(s\) orbital is spherically symmetric and has no preferred direction, so the two spheres necessarily meet along the internuclear axis. This is \(s\)-\(s\) axial overlap, the \(\sigma\) bond of \(\mathrm{H_2}\).

For \(1s\) with \(2p_x\): the lobes of \(2p_x\) point along the \(x\)-axis, that is, along the internuclear axis itself, so the spherical \(1s\) orbital overlaps one lobe end-on. This is \(s\)-\(p\) axial overlap and gives a \(\sigma\) bond.

For \(1s\) with \(2s\): both orbitals are spherically symmetric, so once again the overlap is head-on along the internuclear axis, giving a \(\sigma\) bond.
